screens.title: Single-Cycle and Multi-Cycle Processors
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we study two foundational processor approaches: single-cycle and multi-cycle execution. You will learn the datapath building blocks that every processor uses — the program counter, instruction memory, register file, ALU, data memory, sign-extension, multiplexers, and the control logic — and you will see how those parts are connected in a single-cycle design. We will analyze the critical path: how the longest instruction sets the clock period and why that wastes time for short instructions. Then we examine the multi-cycle alternative that splits an instruction into stages, reuses hardware like the ALU, and shortens the clock period while adding control complexity. Throughout, you will get concrete examples: compute a clock period from component delays, trace a load instruction through five cycles, and contrast where resources are idle or reused. Finally, we connect these ideas to why pipelining became the dominant strategy: it preserves reuse and short clock cycles while allowing many instructions to be in flight. Think about a factory line: is it better to build every product in a single long step, or to move products through specialized stations? That question is the core of this chapter.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to design a single-cycle datapath for a subset of RISC instructions, calculate the clock cycle time by identifying the critical path, explain the limitations that make single-cycle designs inefficient, and design a multi-cycle processor that reuses functional units. These objectives train three complementary skills: structural design, timing analysis, and control sequencing. Designing the datapath trains you to place the program counter, instruction memory, register file, ALU, data memory, sign-extension, and multiplexers so signals flow correctly. Critical-path calculation trains you to add component delays and convert that sum to a clock frequency, which is essential for performance budgeting. Finally, multi-cycle design teaches you to break an instruction into stages and to reason about a simple state machine that emits different control signals each cycle. Each skill matters in real systems: correct datapath design ensures instructions execute as intended, timing analysis constrains clock choices, and control sequencing enables resource reuse. Together they prepare you to understand why pipelining is the next step.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Application
screens.narratorSegment: You will apply the chapter ideas in two practical ways. First, you will design a single-cycle datapath that supports ADD, SUB, AND, OR, LW, SW, and BEQ. That task forces you to choose where multiplexers go and how the register file read and write ports connect. Second, you will calculate a maximum clock frequency for a single-cycle machine using given component delays and then redesign the datapath as a multi-cycle processor with a specified clock cycle. These exercises show the concrete trade-offs: a single long cycle makes even an ADD wait for memory delays, while multi-cycle designs shorten the clock and reuse units but require per-cycle control. Practically, you will learn to trace signals for a load instruction across five cycles, count cycles per instruction, and compare total execution time for a short sequence. These practices build intuition before moving to pipelining, where stage overlap further improves throughput.

screens.title: Single-Cycle Processor: definition and datapath components
screens.narratorSegment: A single-cycle processor completes every instruction in one clock cycle. Practically, that means the datapath contains every functional unit needed by any instruction, and the control unit produces signals that route data through the necessary path for that opcode. Key components are the program counter (PC) to hold addresses, instruction memory to fetch opcodes, a register file with two read ports and one write port, an ALU for arithmetic and address calculation, data memory for loads and stores, a sign extension unit for immediates, and several multiplexers to select between register values, immediates, ALU results, or memory data. For a load, the datapath must fetch the instruction, read register operands, compute the effective address with the ALU, access data memory, then write back to the register. Even if some components are idle for a particular instruction, they must be physically present and connected. A common misconception is that having hardware present implies it is fast; in single-cycle design the clock is set by the slowest possible instruction, so the presence of many units makes the cycle long. A useful mental model is a factory where every product must traverse a long conveyor that includes all machines, whether the product needs them or not. The takeaway: single-cycle designs are simple to reason about but inefficient in time and resource usage.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Single-cycle: every instruction maps through a full datapath and completes in one, long clock cycle.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Single-Cycle
Core Concept

Datapath components

Every component exists simultaneously and signals flow combinationally to produce the correct outputs within one long cycle.

Program Counter (PC)
Holds instruction addresses and increments each cycle.
Instruction Memory
Read-only store of opcodes fetched by PC.
Register File
Two read ports, one write port for operands and results.
ALU & Data Memory
ALU does arithmetic/addressing; data memory holds load/store data.
Multiplexers & Sign-extend
Muxes select register vs immediate and memory vs ALU results; sign-extension prepares immediates for the ALU.
Example: LW instruction path
  1. PC fetches instruction from instruction memory.
  2. Register file read supplies base register.
  3. ALU computes effective address using base + offset.
  4. Data memory reads the word from computed address.
  5. Write back the data into register file.
Key Takeaway

Single-cycle is conceptually simple but forces one cycle to accommodate the slowest instruction.

Common mistake
Assuming the clock can be set by average instruction time. It must accommodate the worst-case critical path.

screens.title: Critical path and clock cycle time
screens.narratorSegment: Critical-path analysis identifies the sequence of components a signal traverses that takes the longest time. In a single-cycle processor the clock period must be at least this longest delay so that all required signals stabilize before the register write occurs. The canonical worst-case for typical RISC datapaths is a load instruction. The path runs from PC to instruction memory to register read to ALU for address calculation to data memory to the multiplexer that selects memory data and then to the register file write. The practical consequence is that a simple ALU-only instruction still waits for the load's long memory delays because the same clock controls everything. To compute a clock period, sum the delays of each component on the critical path. For example, using the provided delays: instruction memory 2 ns, register read 1 ns, ALU 2 ns, data memory 2 ns, multiplexer 0.5 ns, register write 1 ns, the total is 8.5 ns. That yields a maximum clock frequency of about 117.6 MHz. A common misconception is to average delays across instructions; clocks must support the slowest case. The key practical skill is tracing the path, summing delays, and converting to frequency to inform design and compare single-cycle vs multi-cycle choices.

keyIdea.title: Critical path
keyIdea.text: The clock period must be at least the sum of delays along the longest datapath, usually a load instruction in single-cycle designs.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Critical Path
Definition

Trace and compute the longest path

Identify every component the signal traverses from fetch to write-back for the slowest instruction and sum delays.

Critical path (load):
PC → Instruction Memory (2 ns)
→ Register Read (1 ns)
→ ALU (2 ns)
→ Data Memory (2 ns)
→ Mux (0.5 ns)
→ Register Write (1 ns)
Total = 8.5 ns  → Max freq ≈ 1 / 8.5 ns ≈ 117.6 MHz
Pro tip

Always include register write setup and multiplexer delays in the critical path sum.

Explanation bullets
  • Clock period must fit the slowest instruction's total combinational delay.
  • Short instructions cannot use a shorter cycle even if they are faster logically.
  • Component delays are additive; identify memory, ALU, and mux contributions.
  • Designing for worst-case can waste cycles and power for simple instructions.
Analogy
A factory conveyor must be as long as the slowest processing station; every product waits for the longest station even if it doesn't need it.

screens.title: Limitations of single-cycle designs
screens.narratorSegment: Single-cycle processors are attractive for their straightforward control: a combinational decoder maps opcodes directly to control signals that remain stable for one cycle. But that simplicity comes with important costs. First, the clock period must match the slowest instruction, which makes the clock long and slows down otherwise fast instructions. Second, resources are duplicated or permanently present. Data memory and instruction memory coexist, ALU and other units occupy area and consume power even when idle, and multiplexers must be ready to steer data for every instruction. Third, functional units cannot be reused in time because each instruction must complete within one cycle. For example, during the memory read phase of a load, the ALU might be idle, yet the clock must still be long enough to account for memory delays. Another common misconception is that single-cycle designs are always cheaper; while control is simpler, area and power can be worse due to duplicated or always-present hardware. The key trade-off is simplicity versus efficient use of time and silicon. Understanding these limits motivates the switch to multi-cycle and then pipelined designs.

keyIdea.title: Limitations
keyIdea.text: Single-cycle: simple control but slow clock and inefficient resource utilization due to one-cycle worst-case timing.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Single-cycle Limits
Comparison

Simplicity vs inefficiency

Slow clock
Clock must accommodate the slowest instruction, slowing all operations.
Resource presence
Units exist even when idle, increasing area and power use.
No temporal reuse
ALU and memories can’t be time-multiplexed across cycles.
Concrete example

An ADD instruction needs only register read and ALU compute, but it still runs at the load instruction's clock period because clocking is global. This wastes time for simple operations.

Common misconception
Assuming control simplicity implies overall efficiency. Simplicity reduces control logic but can worsen clock and power characteristics.
Key Takeaway

Single-cycle design is great for understanding datapaths but not for high performance or efficient silicon use.

screens.title: Multi-cycle processor: breaking instructions into stages
screens.narratorSegment: A multi-cycle processor splits instruction execution into multiple clock cycles so each cycle does less work and the clock period can be shorter. For example, a typical load instruction can be implemented in five cycles: fetch the instruction and increment the PC, decode and read registers, compute the memory address with the ALU, perform the data memory read, and finally write the data back to the register file. Because the ALU only performs small tasks in each cycle, the clock requirement per cycle is lower. The ALU and other functional units are reused across cycles: the same ALU performs PC increment in the fetch cycle and address calculation in a later cycle. This reuse reduces hardware duplication and can save area and power. The trade-off is control complexity: the control unit must emit different control signals in each cycle, tracked by a state machine or microcode ROM. A common misconception is that multi-cycle always reduces overall latency; for a single load instruction the total time may match a single-cycle design if the product of cycles and shorter clock equals the single-cycle period. The advantage appears in shorter average instruction times and better hardware utilization across a program.

keyIdea.title: Multi-cycle flow
keyIdea.text: Split instruction execution into stages so the clock can be shorter and hardware units can be reused across cycles.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Multi-Cycle
Process Flow

Example: load in five cycles

1
Fetch & PC++
2
Decode & Read Reg
3
ALU: Address Calc
4
Data Memory Read
5
Write Back
Reusing the ALU across cycles means we need only one ALU instance but an FSM to sequence control signals. Memory accesses are separated in time; instruction memory is accessed during fetch and data memory during the memory stage.
Why reuse matters
  • Reduces hardware duplication and area.
  • Shorter clock period since each cycle does less work.
  • Requires FSM or microcode to generate per-cycle control signals.
Check your understanding
If the multi-cycle clock is 2 ns and load takes 5 cycles, is a single load faster or slower than a 10 ns single-cycle design? Do the math to compare.

screens.title: Control complexity: FSM vs Microcode
screens.narratorSegment: Multi-cycle processors require control that changes from cycle to cycle as an instruction progresses through stages. There are two common approaches: a finite-state machine (FSM) that sequences states and outputs control signals per state, or a microcoded control where a microcode ROM stores control words indexed by instruction and current microprogram counter. An FSM is compact and works well for simple instruction sets; it explicitly lists states like FETCH, DECODE, EXECUTE, MEMORY, and WRITEBACK and assigns control outputs at each state. Microcode trades hardware logic for a small ROM and is easier to extend when adding complex instructions. A practical trade-off is clarity versus flexibility: FSMs are fast and simple for RISC designs, while microcode simplifies adding many complex behaviors. A common misconception is that multi-cycle removes control design work; in fact, it shifts complexity from combinational decoding to sequencing logic. When you design the FSM, list each state, the required control signals in that state, and transitions based on instruction fields or completion flags. This explicit sequencing is the reason multi-cycle designs can reuse hardware safely across cycles. Control complexity: FSM vs Microcode means multi-cycle control uses an fsm or microcode to emit different control signals each cycle, enabling safe reuse of hardware units.. In practical terms, how multi-cycle control sequences signals over time. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Multi-cycle control uses an FSM or microcode to emit different control signals each cycle, enabling safe reuse of hardware units.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Control
Architecture

FSM vs Microcode

Finite-State Machine (FSM)
Explicit states like FETCH, DECODE, EXECUTE. Fast and compact for RISC instruction sets.
Microcode
Control words stored in a ROM. Easier to add complex behaviors, trades ROM area for control logic complexity.
Design checklist
  • List needed states for each instruction type.
  • Specify control outputs required in each state.
  • Define transitions based on opcode fields and flags.
  • Decide FSM logic or microcode ROM depending on extensibility needs.
Pro tip

Draw a small table: state × control signals. This makes missing signals or illegal states obvious.

screens.title: Timing example: compute clock frequency from delays
screens.narratorSegment: Let's work a concrete timing example to make critical-path arithmetic tangible. Suppose component delays are: instruction memory 2 ns, register file read 1 ns, ALU 2 ns, data memory 2 ns, multiplexer 0.5 ns, and register file write 1 ns. The load critical path visits these components in sequence. To get the minimum clock period, we sum the delays: 2 plus 1 plus 2 plus 2 plus 0.5 plus 1 equals 8.5 nanoseconds. The maximum clock frequency is the reciprocal: one divided by 8.5 nanoseconds, approximately 117.6 megahertz. Writing this as simple pseudocode helps check each term and avoid omission. A common error is forgetting register write setup or multiplexer propagation. When moving to multi-cycle, designers choose a shorter clock by splitting these tasks into cycles. For example, with a 2 ns multi-cycle clock, five cycles produce the same 10 ns total for a load — equal to some single-cycle clocks — but many short instructions benefit because they need fewer cycles. The practical skill is more than arithmetic: ensure you traced the correct path, included all delays, and compared apples to apples when contrasting designs.

keyIdea.title: Timing example
keyIdea.text: Summing component delays yields clock period; reciprocal gives maximum clock frequency for the single-cycle design.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Timing Example

Critical path arithmetic

// Component delays (ns)
instr_mem = 2.0
reg_read  = 1.0
alu       = 2.0
data_mem  = 2.0
mux       = 0.5
reg_write = 1.0

critical_path = instr_mem + reg_read + alu + data_mem + mux + reg_write
// = 8.5 ns
max_freq_MHz = 1_000 / critical_path  // ≈ 117.6 MHz
Always double-check that you included both memory and register write delays. Small components like multiplexers can shift timing budgets if marginal.
What this means
  • Clock period = 8.5 ns; maximum clock ≈ 117.6 MHz.
  • Short instructions still run at this clock in single-cycle designs.
  • Multi-cycle can shorten per-cycle requirements, allowing a faster clock.
Key Takeaway

Concrete arithmetic yields clear frequency budgets and informs design trade-offs.

screens.title: Hands-on: single-cycle datapath for a RISC subset
screens.narratorSegment: When sketching a single-cycle datapath for a small RISC subset, include the standard components and wires needed so each instruction can complete in a single clock. Start with the program counter feeding instruction memory. Decode the instruction fields into opcode, registers, and immediate. The register file needs two read ports and one write port; connect the read outputs to ALU inputs with a multiplexer on the second ALU input to choose register or sign-extended immediate. Data memory must be present for LW and SW, with an ALU result as address. Add a multiplexer to choose between ALU result and data memory output for writing back to the register file. For branches like BEQ, compare register values and select PC+4 or branch target using a branch control signal. Label the control signals required for each instruction: ALU operation codes, reg write enable, mem read/write enables, mem-to-reg select, and branch. A common error is missing the write-back multiplexer or misconnecting ALU input selection. The exercise prepares you to compute timing by marking the path used by each instruction and locating registers that bound combinational delays.

screens.title: From single-cycle to multi-cycle: trade-offs and timing comparisons
screens.narratorSegment: To compare single-cycle and multi-cycle performance, consider both clock period and cycles per instruction. A single-cycle design uses one cycle per instruction with a long clock period set by the worst-case path. A multi-cycle design uses a shorter clock period because each cycle does less work but requires multiple cycles per instruction. For example, if a single-cycle clock is 10 ns, and a multi-cycle clock is 2 ns, then a load taking 5 cycles in the multi-cycle design also takes 10 ns — the same as the single-cycle load. However, many simple instructions benefit: an ADD that might take one long cycle in the single-cycle design (10 ns) could take fewer multi-cycle cycles whose total is less than 10 ns, giving a speed advantage. The real benefit is program-level: because the multi-cycle design shortens the clock, the average instruction completes faster if most instructions need fewer cycles than the worst-case. Another factor is resource usage and area: multi-cycle reuses units and often saves hardware. The trade-offs are clear: multi-cycle requires more complex control, but it improves clock speed and utilization. When comparing designs, compute total time per instruction type and then weight by expected instruction mix to estimate program performance.

screens.title: Factory metaphor: conveyor vs stations
screens.narratorSegment: A helpful way to internalize these ideas is a factory metaphor. In a single-cycle factory every product moves along the same long conveyor where each station is present on the line whether the product needs it or not. The conveyor takes as long as the slowest station and every product waits for that duration. In a multi-cycle factory, products move between a small set of specialized stations; each product may visit only the stations it needs. Machines are reused in time, which reduces the number of machines required and lets the clock that coordinates station-to-station movement run faster. Importantly, the multi-cycle factory needs a traffic controller: a state machine that tells each product when to move and which machine to use next. A common misconception is to imagine that multi-cycle factories always finish individual long products faster — they do not necessarily shorten the slowest product's end-to-end time, but they improve throughput and utilization across many products. Thinking in these terms helps you reason about ALU reuse, memory access timing, and why pipelining layers concurrency on top of these ideas.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Let's lock in three concise ideas to carry forward. First, the single-cycle datapath contains all functional units and completes every instruction in one clock; this simplicity sets the clock by the slowest instruction and often wastes time. Second, critical-path analysis is the practical method to calculate the clock period: trace the longest combinational path, sum component delays, and take the reciprocal to get maximum frequency. Third, multi-cycle designs split instruction execution into multiple cycles, reuse units like the ALU across cycles, and shorten the clock at the cost of more complex control implemented with an FSM or microcode. Keep the factory metaphor in mind: a single long conveyor versus stations that products visit. These three ideas explain why designers moved from single-cycle to multi-cycle and then to pipelined processors, which add concurrency while preserving reuse benefits.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we study two foundational processor approaches: single-cycle and multi-cycle execution. You will learn the datapath building blocks that every processor uses — the program counter, instruction memory, register file, ALU, data memory, sign-extension, multiplexers, and the control logic — and you will see how those parts are connected in a single-cycle design. We will analyze the critical path: how the longest instruction sets the clock period and why that wastes time for short instructions. Then we examine the multi-cycle alternative that splits an instruction into stages, reuses hardware like the ALU, and shortens the clock period while adding control complexity. Throughout, you will get concrete examples: compute a clock period from component delays, trace a load instruction through five cycles, and contrast where resources are idle or reused. Finally, we connect these ideas to why pipelining became the dominant strategy: it preserves reuse and short clock cycles while allowing many instructions to be in flight. Think about a factory line: is it better to build every product in a single long step, or to move products through specialized stations? That question is the core of this chapter.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to design a single-cycle datapath for a subset of RISC instructions, calculate the clock cycle time by identifying the critical path, explain the limitations that make single-cycle designs inefficient, and design a multi-cycle processor that reuses functional units. These objectives train three complementary skills: structural design, timing analysis, and control sequencing. Designing the datapath trains you to place the program counter, instruction memory, register file, ALU, data memory, sign-extension, and multiplexers so signals flow correctly. Critical-path calculation trains you to add component delays and convert that sum to a clock frequency, which is essential for performance budgeting. Finally, multi-cycle design teaches you to break an instruction into stages and to reason about a simple state machine that emits different control signals each cycle. Each skill matters in real systems: correct datapath design ensures instructions execute as intended, timing analysis constrains clock choices, and control sequencing enables resource reuse. Together they prepare you to understand why pipelining is the next step.

You will apply the chapter ideas in two practical ways. First, you will design a single-cycle datapath that supports ADD, SUB, AND, OR, LW, SW, and BEQ. That task forces you to choose where multiplexers go and how the register file read and write ports connect. Second, you will calculate a maximum clock frequency for a single-cycle machine using given component delays and then redesign the datapath as a multi-cycle processor with a specified clock cycle. These exercises show the concrete trade-offs: a single long cycle makes even an ADD wait for memory delays, while multi-cycle designs shorten the clock and reuse units but require per-cycle control. Practically, you will learn to trace signals for a load instruction across five cycles, count cycles per instruction, and compare total execution time for a short sequence. These practices build intuition before moving to pipelining, where stage overlap further improves throughput.

A single-cycle processor completes every instruction in one clock cycle. Practically, that means the datapath contains every functional unit needed by any instruction, and the control unit produces signals that route data through the necessary path for that opcode. Key components are the program counter (PC) to hold addresses, instruction memory to fetch opcodes, a register file with two read ports and one write port, an ALU for arithmetic and address calculation, data memory for loads and stores, a sign extension unit for immediates, and several multiplexers to select between register values, immediates, ALU results, or memory data. For a load, the datapath must fetch the instruction, read register operands, compute the effective address with the ALU, access data memory, then write back to the register. Even if some components are idle for a particular instruction, they must be physically present and connected. A common misconception is that having hardware present implies it is fast; in single-cycle design the clock is set by the slowest possible instruction, so the presence of many units makes the cycle long. A useful mental model is a factory where every product must traverse a long conveyor that includes all machines, whether the product needs them or not. The takeaway: single-cycle designs are simple to reason about but inefficient in time and resource usage.

Critical-path analysis identifies the sequence of components a signal traverses that takes the longest time. In a single-cycle processor the clock period must be at least this longest delay so that all required signals stabilize before the register write occurs. The canonical worst-case for typical RISC datapaths is a load instruction. The path runs from PC to instruction memory to register read to ALU for address calculation to data memory to the multiplexer that selects memory data and then to the register file write. The practical consequence is that a simple ALU-only instruction still waits for the load's long memory delays because the same clock controls everything. To compute a clock period, sum the delays of each component on the critical path. For example, using the provided delays: instruction memory 2 ns, register read 1 ns, ALU 2 ns, data memory 2 ns, multiplexer 0.5 ns, register write 1 ns, the total is 8.5 ns. That yields a maximum clock frequency of about 117.6 MHz. A common misconception is to average delays across instructions; clocks must support the slowest case. The key practical skill is tracing the path, summing delays, and converting to frequency to inform design and compare single-cycle vs multi-cycle choices.

Single-cycle processors are attractive for their straightforward control: a combinational decoder maps opcodes directly to control signals that remain stable for one cycle. But that simplicity comes with important costs. First, the clock period must match the slowest instruction, which makes the clock long and slows down otherwise fast instructions. Second, resources are duplicated or permanently present. Data memory and instruction memory coexist, ALU and other units occupy area and consume power even when idle, and multiplexers must be ready to steer data for every instruction. Third, functional units cannot be reused in time because each instruction must complete within one cycle. For example, during the memory read phase of a load, the ALU might be idle, yet the clock must still be long enough to account for memory delays. Another common misconception is that single-cycle designs are always cheaper; while control is simpler, area and power can be worse due to duplicated or always-present hardware. The key trade-off is simplicity versus efficient use of time and silicon. Understanding these limits motivates the switch to multi-cycle and then pipelined designs.

A multi-cycle processor splits instruction execution into multiple clock cycles so each cycle does less work and the clock period can be shorter. For example, a typical load instruction can be implemented in five cycles: fetch the instruction and increment the PC, decode and read registers, compute the memory address with the ALU, perform the data memory read, and finally write the data back to the register file. Because the ALU only performs small tasks in each cycle, the clock requirement per cycle is lower. The ALU and other functional units are reused across cycles: the same ALU performs PC increment in the fetch cycle and address calculation in a later cycle. This reuse reduces hardware duplication and can save area and power. The trade-off is control complexity: the control unit must emit different control signals in each cycle, tracked by a state machine or microcode ROM. A common misconception is that multi-cycle always reduces overall latency; for a single load instruction the total time may match a single-cycle design if the product of cycles and shorter clock equals the single-cycle period. The advantage appears in shorter average instruction times and better hardware utilization across a program.

Multi-cycle processors require control that changes from cycle to cycle as an instruction progresses through stages. There are two common approaches: a finite-state machine (FSM) that sequences states and outputs control signals per state, or a microcoded control where a microcode ROM stores control words indexed by instruction and current microprogram counter. An FSM is compact and works well for simple instruction sets; it explicitly lists states like FETCH, DECODE, EXECUTE, MEMORY, and WRITEBACK and assigns control outputs at each state. Microcode trades hardware logic for a small ROM and is easier to extend when adding complex instructions. A practical trade-off is clarity versus flexibility: FSMs are fast and simple for RISC designs, while microcode simplifies adding many complex behaviors. A common misconception is that multi-cycle removes control design work; in fact, it shifts complexity from combinational decoding to sequencing logic. When you design the FSM, list each state, the required control signals in that state, and transitions based on instruction fields or completion flags. This explicit sequencing is the reason multi-cycle designs can reuse hardware safely across cycles. Control complexity: FSM vs Microcode means multi-cycle control uses an fsm or microcode to emit different control signals each cycle, enabling safe reuse of hardware units.. In practical terms, how multi-cycle control sequences signals over time. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's work a concrete timing example to make critical-path arithmetic tangible. Suppose component delays are: instruction memory 2 ns, register file read 1 ns, ALU 2 ns, data memory 2 ns, multiplexer 0.5 ns, and register file write 1 ns. The load critical path visits these components in sequence. To get the minimum clock period, we sum the delays: 2 plus 1 plus 2 plus 2 plus 0.5 plus 1 equals 8.5 nanoseconds. The maximum clock frequency is the reciprocal: one divided by 8.5 nanoseconds, approximately 117.6 megahertz. Writing this as simple pseudocode helps check each term and avoid omission. A common error is forgetting register write setup or multiplexer propagation. When moving to multi-cycle, designers choose a shorter clock by splitting these tasks into cycles. For example, with a 2 ns multi-cycle clock, five cycles produce the same 10 ns total for a load — equal to some single-cycle clocks — but many short instructions benefit because they need fewer cycles. The practical skill is more than arithmetic: ensure you traced the correct path, included all delays, and compared apples to apples when contrasting designs.
